power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Background: Recruitment is often a challenge in health behaviour surveillance studies, especially when working with young children.

The International Study of Movement Behaviours in the Early Years (SUNRISE Study) creates a unique opportunity to explore how barriers to recruitment and subsequent recruitment rates vary across countries.
The present study aimed to examine global differences in recruitment rates, identify prominent barriers to recruitment, and explore researchers' perceptions of recruitment practices.

Methods: Research teams from 48 countries participating in the SUNRISE Study completed an online survey to examine perceived barriers and facilitators to recruitment of early childhood education and care (ECEC) settings, parents and preschoolers in the SUNRISE study.

Descriptive analyses were performed to examine recruitment rates and barriers across countries, and directed content analysis, guided by the socio-ecological model were used to identify researchers' perceptions of effective facilitators to overcome barriers.

Results: Significant differences in recruitment rates and barriers were observed at both the country income and geographical region level for ECEC and parent/child recruitment with European and high-income countries reporting significantly lower recruitment rates.
Across countries, the main barrier to ECEC and parent/child recruitment was time commitment concerns and parental concerns regarding accelerometer use, respectively.

At the ECEC level, organisational barriers and centre beliefs regarding parent willingness were also identified to be prominent barriers by African & Eastern-Mediterranean, South-East Asia & Western Pacific, and Americas regions.
text.formatted: At the ECEC level, organisational barriers and centre beliefs regarding parent willingness were also identified to be prominent barriers by African & Eastern-Mediterranean, South-East Asia & Western Pacific, and Americas regions.

text.text: These barriers were also considered prominent by low & lower-middle-income and upper-middle-income countries.
text.formatted: These barriers were also considered prominent by low & lower-middle-income and upper-middle-income countries.

text.text: Additional barriers to parent/child recruitment were time commitment concerns and lack of interest, as identified by European and high-income countries.
Globally, facilitators at intrapersonal, interpersonal, and community level were found to be beneficial in overcoming recruitment barriers.

This may involve providing education on the importance of movement behaviours to improve understanding, delivering participants in-person information sessions, and enlisting community organisations and professional networks to aid recruitment.
Conclusion: Recruitment for child health surveillance and accelerometery research is inherently complex and may require context-specific approaches to overcome barriers.

Our findings provide context-specific recruitment approaches to support the design and implementation of future global surveillance recruitment strategies, and to help ensure greater representativeness in global health research.

text.text: Therefore, additional considerations need to be made around differing cultural contexts impacting recruitment and study implementation; utilising data collection instruments that are appropriate for global measurement; and informed consent/assent and ethical challenges of data collection with diverse child populations (11, 12).

text.text: Furthermore, methodological challenges arise from varying ethical requirements across countries such as the distinction between active and passive parental consent, which can lead to inconsistent response rates and potential non-response bias, which complicates cross-national comparisons (13, 14).

text.text: This demonstrates a need for robust planning and continual methodological review from initial study design through to data analysis and dissemination of findings.
Early childhood education and care (ECEC) settings are often a primary setting when recruiting participants and implementing child-based research.

ECEC settings can provide many advantages such as convenience, better retention rates, a diverse range of participants from the target population, and can allow education staff to aid in the recruitment of parents and children (15) (16) (17).

text.text: However, utilising ECEC settings for recruitment can also bring about many challenges.
For example, multiple levels of approval are often required before accessing ECEC settings and parents and children can then be contacted (18, 19).

text.text: This process can often be lengthy and complex resulting in delays in research timelines, or even blocked access.

Additionally, utilising ECEC settings may bring about challenges specific to educational settings such as curricula constraints, lack of staff, and lack of space or resources which researchers also need to consider and navigate throughout recruitment processes (16, 19).

text.text: Regarding parental challenges, utilising educational and care settings, such as ECEC, to recruit may limit contact opportunities with parents, resulting in mistrust and difficulty obtaining parental consent (16, 18).

text.text: Furthermore, health surveillance research has often employed the use of self-report measures despite the validity and reliability of these measures being questioned.
As such, the use of device-based measurement tools, such as accelerometery, is becoming increasingly popular for health surveillance research.

Though this approach may also bring about challenges due to the novelty and unfamiliarity of these devices to participants, and the increased cost in comparison to subjective measures for researchers (1).

text.text: While it is important to recognise these challenges, it is equally important to identify specific barriers to health surveillance and accelerometery research, how these barriers may impact recruitment rates and identify facilitators to overcome barriers in addition to how this may vary across countries-a research area that is limited in the current literature.
The SUNRISE Study is a global surveillance study of 24-hr movement behaviours in children aged 3 -4 years across 66 countries (24).

text.text: The study implements a standardised, robust protocol, employing the use of accelerometery to collect data on the 24-hr movement behaviours, across diverse settings.

This provides a unique opportunity to evaluate how global research processes and measurement instruments (particularly the use of accelerometery) perform across different cultural, political and geographical landscapes (24).

text.text: As with all global studies, recruitment rates and challenges encountered differ greatly between countries.

Some evidence from the SUNRISE pilot phase studies highlights that, while the protocol is robust, research must still navigate significant practical hurdles, including technical issues with device-based measurements, parental concern on the use of device-based measurement tools, the reliance on parental-proxy reporting, and the complexities of local ethics approval (25) (26) (27).

text.text: However, the full extent of the various recruitment barriers and differences in recruitment rates has not been explored systematically.
In doing so, valuable insights on the practicalities of recruitment in large-scale international child health surveillance studies and studies that employ the use of accelerometery, may be provided.

Therefore, the aims of this study were to (a) examine differences in recruitment rates of ECEC settings and parent/child dyads at global, regional, and country income levels, (b) identify researchers perceived barriers to recruitment, and (c) explore perceptions of effective facilitators to overcome prominent barriers.

The present study was conducted as part of the SUNRISE Study and adopts a mixed-methods approach to gather insights into recruitment rates, barriers to the recruitment of ECEC settings and parent/child dyads, and researchers' perceptions of facilitators to overcome prominent barriers.

The SUNRISE Study brings together researchers from countries across the globe to monitor adherence to the WHO Guidelines on Physical Activity, Sedentary Behaviour, and Sleep for Children Under 5 Years of Age.
Currently, there are 66 countries are involved in the SUNRISE study with 22 of high-income, 19 of upper-middle income, and 25 of low and lower-middle income.
The SUNRISE Study comprises of a pilot study and main study phase.
The pilot study aims to determine the feasibility of recruiting 100 male and female children from urban and rural settings and to test the feasibility and acceptability of the standardised protocol.
The main study aims to recruit 1000 children (sex-balanced) from rural and urban settings to determine the proportion of children who meet the WHO Global Guidelines (24).

text.text: At the time of data collection (September 2025), a total of 51 countries participating in the SUNRISE Study were in the process of completing, or had completed, the pilot or main study phase.
The research team for these countries were asked to complete an online questionnaire to gather relevant information.
The questionnaire was to be completed once for each study phase (pilot and main) where applicable.

Data were collected through an online questionnaire consisting of both open-and closedended questions, administered through the REDCap platform, a secure web-based application designed to support data capture for research studies (24, 28).

text.text: An initial survey collected data regarding barriers to recruitment and facilitators to overcome barriers between September and November 2025.

As this initial survey did not gather information regarding recruitment rates, a follow-up survey was provided to gain insight into the recruitment rates of ECEC settings and parent/child dyads between February and May 2026.
A copy of both surveys is provided in Additional File 1.

Descriptive analyses were conducted to provide summaries of recruitment rates and barriers to recruitment at a global level and according to WHO region and World Bank income categories at the time of country data collection.
Regional and income categories were collapsed to allow for an appropriate sample size for analyses and interpretation in each group.
Therefore, regional categories include African & Eastern-Mediterranean (AF-EM), Americas (AM), South-East Asia & Western-Pacific (SEA-WP), and European (EU).

text.text: Recruitment rates and barriers were discussed for ECEC recruitment and parent/child recruitment.
ECEC recruitment rates were calculated as a percentage by dividing the total number of settings that were contacted by the number of settings that participated.

The recruitment rates of parents/children were then calculated as a percentage by dividing the total number of eligible parents/children in each participating ECEC setting by the number of parent/child dyads that participated.
Kruskal-Wallis analyses were used to compare recruitment rates across regional and income categories.
Follow-up Dunn's pairwise comparisons were conducted applying Bonferroni corrections to test for significant differences between groups.
Rank-biserial (rrb) correlation effect sizes were calculated for pairwise comparisons, rrb = 1 -2U/(n1*n2).
A small effect size is defined as ≥ .11, a medium effect size is ≥ .28, and a large effect size is ≥ .43 (29).

Barriers to ECEC Recruitment.
At a global level, concerns for time commitment of involvement in the SUNRISE Study was indicated as the most prominent barrier to recruitment.
However, differences were observed at both regional and country income levels.

ECEC concerns for parent/child willingness to participate was indicated as the biggest barrier by both AF-EM and LLMIC and bureaucratic or institutional barriers was indicated by SEA-WP and UMIC as the biggest barrier.
In addition to time commitment concerns, AM ECEC settings also indicated bureaucratic or institutional barriers to also impact recruitment.
Lastly, EU and HIC ECEC settings indicated concerns for time commitment of involvement as the biggest barrier.
At a global level, the biggest barrier to the recruitment of parents/children was parental concerns around child wearing an accelerometer device to collect movement behaviour data.
This barrier was also reported to have the biggest impact on recruitment by AF-EM, AM, SEA-WP, LLMIC, and UMIC.
However, both EU and HIC indicated that parental lack of interest and concerns for time commitment of involvement was more influential to recruitment.

At a global level, 43% (n = 26) of responses indicated that facilitators at the interpersonal level were the most beneficial in overcoming ECEC-related barriers followed by facilitators at the community level as indicated by 25% (n = 15) of responses.
Facilitators at the intrapersonal and public policy levels were indicated by 10% (n = 6) of responses and facilitators at the organisational level by 7% (n = 4) of responses.
Lastly, 3% (n = 2) of responses indicated that barriers could not be overcome or did not provide insight into facilitators to overcome experienced barriers.
Across regions, interpersonal facilitators were more commonly applied to overcome barriers by AF-EM and SEA-WP.

Differences were observed in AM and EU where AM indicated facilitators at the community level promoted recruitment in addition to facilitators at the interpersonal level whilst EU more commonly only adopted facilitators at the community level to overcome ECEC barriers.
All income categories perceived facilitators at the interpersonal level to be beneficial in overcoming ECEC barriers.

Regarding facilitators to overcome parent/childrelated barriers, 46% (n = 28) of responses perceived facilitators at the interpersonal level to be a successful strategy to overcome barriers closely followed by facilitators at the intrapersonal level, as indicated by 44% (n = 27) of responses.

Facilitators at the community level were only perceived to be beneficial by 3% (n = 2) of responses whilst facilitators at the organisational and public policy level were not perceived to be effective for parent/child recruitment.
Lastly, 5% (n = 3) of responses indicated that parent/child barriers could not be overcome whilst 2% (n = 1) of responses did not provide insight into facilitators.

Across regions, AF-EM, AM, and SEA-WP suggested that facilitators at the intrapersonal level were successful in overcoming parent/child barriers whilst EU suggested facilitators at the interpersonal level to be more influential.

Across income categories, facilitators at the intrapersonal level were used to overcome parent/child barriers by LLMIC whilst UMIC and HIC more commonly applied facilitators at the interpersonal level.

text.text: The aim of this study was to identify and discuss global differences in recruitment rates in the SUNRISE Study, identify barriers to recruitment and differences experienced between regions and income categories, and to explore researchers' perceptions of effective facilitators to overcome prominent barriers.
Recruitment rates across categories were mixed, however, SEA-WP and AF-EM generally had higher recruitment rates for both ECEC and parent/child recruitment.
Barriers to recruitment were also mixed.
Whilst ECEC concerns for time commitment of involvement to participate was the biggest barrier at the global level, many differences were observed across regional and country income levels.
Barriers to parent/child recruitment were less diverse with parental concern around their child wearing an accelerometer was generally reported as the biggest barrier.
Lastly, researchers perceived facilitators at the interpersonal level as a successful strategy to overcome both ECEC and parent/child barriers experienced.
However, these strategies may be improved when applying more context-specific related facilitators.
Findings from the present study suggested that AF-EM, SEA-WP, and LLMIC had generally higher recruitment rates.

It is important to note that global differences in recruitment rates in global health surveillance studies can be impacted by several factors such as differences in varying regulatory frameworks, infrastructural gaps, socioeconomic status, cultural norms, and research participation novelty or fatigue.
Differences in regulatory frameworks may explain the difference observed between regions.

A range of ethical approval processes are required before participating in research which vary by country and may consist of minimal procedures to highly complex procedures which require ethical approval at multiple stages.
For example, Scotland requires consent to firstly be obtained from the local government authority before ECEC settings within that area can be contacted.

Similarly, the European Union introduced the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) which adopts strict privacy laws in the collection, processing, and storage of health data in member countries (34).

Research conducted with young children also requires both parent consent and child assent to ensure children are adequately protected (41).

text.text: As young children's selfdetermination is not yet matured, the principle of respect ensures that children are protected by requiring permission from parents or legal guardians whilst still providing children with the opportunity to engage in and develop self-determination.
Child assent involved the explanation of participation in an appropriate manner and children subsequently deciding whether they would wish to take part.

However, parental consent is more complex, requiring parents to be adequately informed of the nature and purpose of the research, any risks or benefits expected from participation, and information regarding data protection, before written consent can be obtained (41, 42).

text.text: The additional requirements of including data protection information forms add to the already lengthy and complex parental consent forms, which may add to parent burden and lack of understanding resulting in parents possibly being deterred from participation in early stages.

Considering the differences observed between country income levels, the present study found that LLMIC reported higher recruitment rates than HIC for ECEC recruitment and both LLMIC and UMIC reported higher recruitment rates than HIC for parent/child recruitment.

This finding may be explained by the overrepresentation of HIC in public health research, resulting in these countries being overwhelmed with opportunities to participate in research and having to be more selective in what they participate in (43, 44).

text.text: In contrast, LLMICs may see research participation as a novel and exciting opportunity.
Furthermore, current literature indicates that a high proportion of research on the 24-hr movement behaviours in preschool children is conducted in HICs (5, 45).
text.formatted: Furthermore, current literature indicates that a high proportion of research on the 24-hr movement behaviours in preschool children is conducted in HICs <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(5,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">45)</ref>.

text.text: The SUNRISE Study aims to overcome this research inequality by limiting the recruitment of HICs into the study-over one third of participating countries being of low-income.
SUNRISE provides these countries novel insights into the movement behaviours of their young children, information which may not be as easily accessible through health services in comparison to HICs.

Therefore, parents from LLMICs may be more willing to participate in health surveillance research as they view it as being beneficial to their child, offering a possible explanation to the differences observed in recruitment rates.

Furthermore, LLMIC indicated that facilitators at the intrapersonal level were successful in overcoming parent/child barriers to recruitment which focussed on ensuring participants fully understand the nature and importance of the study before consent was obtained.
Employing these facilitators may also build strong trust and rapport between researchers and parents and children.

In doing so, concerns could be adequately addressed, and parents may have obtained a stronger understanding than those from HIC where facilitators at the interpersonal level were more heavily adopted.

Whilst interpersonal facilitators are beneficial in providing adequate communication, such strategies may assume parents already have a basic understanding of the importance of research participation.
Looking at barriers to ECEC recruitment, concerns for time commitment of involvement and bureaucratic or institutional barriers were a challenge.
Research participation may bring about additional burdens to ECEC practitioners.

A previous study reported that school leaders, such as head teachers, refused to participate in research due to time constraints, perceived burden, concerns for student wellbeing, or a lack of alignment with institutional priorities (20).

text.text: Despite common barriers to ECEC recruitment being organisational barriers, researchers involved in the SUNRISE Study indicated that interpersonal strategies were successful in overcoming ECEC barriers.

Such strategies focus on the importance of establishing strong relationships between the research team and prospective ECEC settings to build trust and rapport allowing for meaningful interactions to occur which subsequently supported recruitment.

Similar findings have been reported in previous research that aimed to identify successful strategies to "Recruit, engage, and retain children in behavioural health risk factor studies" (REACH), where building trustful relationships was also identified as a successful strategy (49) and face-to-face recruitment approaches were most suitable in order to build relationships (50).

text.text: However, prominent barriers to ECEC recruitment referred to concern for time commitment of involvement and bureaucratic or institutional barriers.
Whilst interpersonal strategies may be useful in first obtaining a strong relationship with ECEC settings, more specific organisational strategies may be better equipped to overcome such barriers.
For example, logistical barriers such as staff shortages, high staff workload, and daily schedule requirements (51) are possible reasons as to why ECEC may decline participation in research.

Therefore, organisational strategies which focus on working closely with key staff members to discuss their concerns and create flexible participation procedures which minimise staff burden and ensure minimal disruptions to daily activities may facilitate participation more successfully than interpersonal strategies alone.
ECEC incentives, including financial compensation for staff time, may also be a successful strategy when resources are available.

Regarding barriers to parent/child recruitment, concerns around child wearing an accelerometer was reported as the biggest barrier overall and by AF-EM, AM, and SEA-WP countries, and by LLMIC and UMIC.

The use of accelerometery to assess movement behaviours has become an increasingly popular measure providing an alternative to traditional self-report measures which often raise questions regarding reliability and validity of results (1, 52).
text.formatted: The use of accelerometery to assess movement behaviours has become an increasingly popular measure providing an alternative to traditional self-report measures which often raise questions regarding reliability and validity of results <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(1,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">52)</ref>.

text.text: Previous evidence has suggested that the use of self-reporting measures in national health surveys may produce misleading data resulting in unintended adverse consequences for public health policy.

Limitations to such measures call for a focus on moving towards device-based surveillance systems, especially in national and international research where comparisons of movement behaviours can be made more easily (1, 53).

text.text: However, previous research has suggested that parents may be hesitant to use device-based measurement tools due to concerns regarding the device being lost or broken, the use of large devices possibly having a negative impact on their child's sleep, the device having direct contact with the skin, and safety and privacy concerns (54).

text.text: Further research has suggested the importance of establishing trust with parents through face-to-face interactions may aid in alleviating such concerns (55, 56).

text.text: These interactions allow researchers to discuss and demonstrate the use of these devices to address concerns and allow parents to understand why and how the device is used.

Despite device-based concerns being a barrier at a global level, EU countries and HICs indicated that parental lack of interest and concerns for time commitment of involvement to be a more influential parent/child recruitment barrier.

Such barriers have been reported in nutrition, PA, and obesity interventions where time constraints and lack of understanding and the complexity of information were prominent barriers to participation (23).

text.text: EU countries and HICs may have additional work and family commitments that may deter parents and children from participating in research if they view the time commitment of involvement to be burdensome (23, 57, 58).

text.text: Strategies at interpersonal level were also indicated as successful facilitators to overcome parent/child barriers globally.
Again, building trust and rapport between researchers and parents is important and may best be done through in-person visits and conducting information sessions.

However, when looking at regional-and country income-level responses, only EU countries, UMICs, and HICs reported interpersonal strategies whilst AF-EM, AM, and SEA-WP countries and LLMICs indicated intrapersonal strategies to be more beneficial.
This may be linked to the prominent barriers experienced by some regions and income categories.
For example, AF-EM, AM, and SEA-WP countries, and LLMICs and UMICs reported concerns around child wearing an accelerometer as the most prominent barrier as noted above.

Strategies at intrapersonal level may be better suited to overcome such barriers as these strategies focused on providing parents with adequate education and information on the nature, purpose, and methods of the research.
The use of accelerometery may be novel to parents resulting in hesitations around allowing their child to wear the device.
By providing parents with details and examples on how and why the devices are used may alleviate their concerns and facilitate participation.
Parent/child incentives, including providing child-level movement behaviour reports, may also be a successful strategy when resources are available.
Recruitment of participants to health surveillance studies involving the childhood population and accelerometery is inherently complex and requires the consideration of multiple factors.
Ultimately, successful recruitment of both ECEC and parent/child dyads requires potential participants having a clear understanding on the value of the study topic and their involvement.
Across all regions and income categories, it should not be assumed that participants are knowledgeable on 24-hr movement behaviours.
Research teams involved in recruitment should ensure that both ECEC settings and parents understand the nature and importance of the study's objectives.
This approach to recruitment creates trust between the research team, ECEC settings, and parents.
It also ensures participants hold the required knowledge and understanding of the importance of the research to be able to provide fully informed consent.

This approach may also be specifically relevant when the use of accelerometers is a large barrier as this measurement tool may be uncommon to participants resulting in many concerns regarding its use.

Addressing the concerns effectively may be achieved through holding in-person information sessions with participants allowing researchers to thoroughly show and explain how the device works and address participant concerns efficiently.
Recommendations to overcome ECEC-specific barriers are more complex with differences being observed across regional and income categories.
Generally, it can be recommended that recruitment of ECEC settings may be improved by receiving support from higher-level government departments or organisations.
This support may encourage ECEC settings to participate if the research is viewed as being trusted by such departments.
Additionally, it is important to be flexible in the data collection procedures by taking into consideration specific time or staff constraints experienced by ECEC settings.
Future research and surveillance should plan recruitment strategies taking into consideration barriers they may encounter, both globally and locally.
In doing so, recruitment processes may become more efficient and result in more representative samples.
An initial recruitment strategy may be developed during pilot work with the subsequent strategy for main study recruitment being enhanced by knowledge and experience gained throughout the pilot (36).

text.text: This allows countries to identify specific barriers they may encounter during their own recruitment processes which can be addressed using suggested facilitators identified from the present study to help make recruitment processes more efficient.

The present study collected data from the SUNRISE study, a real-world international accelerometery based surveillance study on the 24-hr movement behaviours of preschool children, to gain insight into global differences in recruitment rates and researchers perceived barriers and facilitators to recruitment.

In doing so, the study offers a novel multi-country perspective to provide insights into the recruitment processes of a global surveillance study and the use of accelerometery across diverse international contexts.

Further, the study provides a more comprehensive understanding into barriers encountered and identifies possible facilitators that may promote recruitment in future global health surveillance and accelerometery research.
Nonetheless, this study is not without limitations.
One limitation is the small sample size of this study for statistical comparison.
Given the small sample size and the absence of prespecified hypotheses regarding regional and income group differences, these findings should be considered exploratory and interpreted with caution.
Further research is needed into group differences in recruitment rates in international surveillance of 24-hour movement behaviours.

Another limitation refers to the data reported were collected through self-report surveys completed by SUNRISE researchers resulting in findings being subjective to the experiences of these researchers.
Therefore, whilst the results may provide insights into facilitators to overcome barriers and improve recruitment, these findings may not be generalisable outside the SUNRISE study.
Despite this, the SUNRISE study provided a unique opportunity to capture insights from respondents across a wide geographical and income landscape.

Lastly, contextual factors which were not captured in the present study, such as differences in policy, culture, resources available, use of incentives, and recruitment duration, may also influence recruitment rates.
Further research is required to identify the impact of these factors to gain a better understanding into recruitment.

As the present research only collects data regarding the perceptions of the SUNRISE study researchers, additional research is required to gain insight into parent and ECEC staff perceptions of barriers which result in them declining participation to research and strategies which would aid in the promotion of their participation.
This further research would allow more context-specific recommendations, considering a whole-systems approach to recruitment and participation in research.

The present study identified global differences in recruitment rates, identified top barriers to ECEC and parent/child recruitment across global, regional, and country income levels, and identified potential facilitators to overcome prominent barriers.
Concerns regarding time commitment and accelerometer use were prominent ECEC and parent/child barriers, respectively.
Facilitators at interpersonal level to overcome barriers were indicated by researchers to be successful in overcoming both ECEC and parent/child barriers.
However, these strategies may be improved with more context-specific approaches, such as organisational strategies for ECEC recruitment and intrapersonal strategies for parent/child recruitment.
Additional factors may also impact recruitment resulting in recruitment procedures being inherently complex requiring flexible, context-specific approaches to promote recruitment.

These findings aim to provide context-specific recruitment approaches to support the design and implementation of future global surveillance recruitment strategies to help research findings be more representative and recruitment elements of research are more efficient.

The responses will be used to inform an upcoming publication on global recruitment for the SUNRISE study.
These findings will support future SUNRISE countries and other global surveillance studies with their own study recruitment.
